reading_2_parser.note: the parser reads the unit from the PART string (the quantity field has none); 'unit recognised' therefore counts food names that begin with a unit word (e.g. a count noun), not stated units

reading_3_name_field.note: single-letter t and c excluded by the lexicon; count nouns such as clove or can are unit tokens, so this is an upper bound

reading_4_ner_counts_S174.note: model-derived (DeBERTa-CRF), per-span output not on this server; Wikibooks 82.2 % and TASTEset 83.7 % in the same file

verdict.consequence: Every Food.com quantity is a bare count or a bare number (no mass, no volume): grams are UNKNOWN by construction, and no parser change (including SP-002) can create them.
verdict.statement: No Food.com quantity string contains a letter, so no unit token exists in the quantity field for a parser to lose: the unit drop is source-level. The parser recognises a unit on 0.198 % of lines, the name field holds a unit word on 4.244 % of strings and the NER finds UNIT spans on 4.161 % of lines: all three are well below 5 % and come from words inside food names, not from a stated unit. The NER's UNIT span count and the number of name strings holding a unit word agree within about 2 %, and its QUANTITY span count equals the number of lines that start with a digit to within 0.01 %.
